title: Armendariz v. Foundation Health Psychcare Services, Inc.
lead: Two discharged supervisors challenged an arbitration agreement that restricted their remedies and covered their termination claims without covering corresponding employer claims. California allowed arbitration preserving statutory rights but refused to enforce this arrangement because its combined defects could not be cured by deleting terms.

actors.name: Marybeth Armendariz and Dolores Olague-Rodgers
actors.role: Discharged supervisors alleging discrimination and wrongful termination

actors.name: Justice Brown
actors.role: Concurring Justice disagreeing on cost allocation, joined by Chin

proceedings: The trial court refused arbitration; the Court of Appeal would enforce the agreement after severance. The California Supreme Court reversed and directed affirmance of the trial court’s judgment on August 24, 2000.
limits: The court decided enforceability, not discrimination liability. It reserved Federal Arbitration Act coverage, sufficient notice of statutory-claim coverage, the precise review standard for an award, and whether the remedy restriction alone required total rejection.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Employment began with a mandatory termination clause
sections.cue: Introduce the employees and the actual scope of the writing.
paragraphs: Foundation Health Psychcare Services hired Marybeth Armendariz and Dolores Olague-Rodgers into its Provider Relations Group in July and August 1995. They later became supervisors earning $38,000 annually. Both signed application forms and later separate agreements requiring arbitration of contentions that termination was wrongful, violated employment conditions or an express or implied term or covenant, or otherwise violated their rights. Signing was a condition of employment.

The clause incorporated California arbitration statutes but limited the exclusive remedy to wages between discharge and the award, excluding every other legal or equitable remedy, including reinstatement and injunctions. It therefore restricted relief as well as selecting a forum. Although both parties agreed to submit the described matter, that matter was the employee’s wrongful-termination claim, not corresponding employer claims or every conceivable employee claim.

On June 20, 1996, the employer said the positions were eliminated and discharged both women. They alleged sexual harassment and discrimination during employment and discharge because of actual or perceived heterosexual orientation. These were claims, not findings; same-sex harassment was recognized as unlawful under the governing statute.

sections.title: The courts differed over whether severance could save arbitration
sections.cue: Trace the requested relief and lower rulings.
paragraphs: The employees sued under California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act, or FEHA, and asserted three additional tort and contract causes for wrongful termination. They requested general and punitive damages, injunctions, attorney fees, and costs. Foundation Health moved to compel arbitration under Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2.

After declarations, the trial court found an adhesive agreement with one-sided employee-only arbitration and backpay-only relief, and identified a supposed discovery deficiency. It declined to excise isolated terms from the overall unfair arrangement. The Court of Appeal agreed about adhesion and the unlawful damages limit but favored enforcing the remainder; it considered the incorporated California Arbitration Act sufficient for discovery.

The employees challenged both mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims generally and this agreement’s discovery, review, costs, remedies, and mutuality. The employer sought construction or severance of disputed terms and argued these comparatively low-level positions explained omission of employer claims.

sections.title: Statutory rights could move to arbitration but not disappear
sections.cue: Explain arbitrability and the reserved federal question.
paragraphs: Justice Mosk’s majority rejected Duffield, the Ninth Circuit decision reading the Civil Rights Act of 1991 to prohibit mandatory arbitration of Title VII and equivalent claims. Congress had encouraged arbitration where appropriate and authorized by law without express prohibition. Gilmer, the earlier Supreme Court decision allowing statutory employment arbitration, made silent incorporation of a categorical bar unlikely. Prior collective-bargaining cases involved different tensions between collective representation and individual rights. No California enactment categorically prohibited FEHA arbitration either.

The court did not decide whether the Federal Arbitration Act’s employment exemption applied, because California’s Act independently enforced agreements subject to ordinary contract defenses and lacked that exemption. It likewise reserved whether this wording adequately notified employees that statutory claims were included. State enforcement-agency remedies and independent functions remained available.

Civil Code sections 1668 and 3513 barred agreements exempting legal violations or overriding laws established for public purposes. FEHA served such purposes. Drawing on Cole, an employment-arbitration precedent, the court required neutral arbitrators, sufficient discovery, a written award, full statutory remedies, and access without improper forum costs. Neutrality was not disputed. The safeguards addressed compulsory employment arbitration, leaving genuinely voluntary postdispute procedural bargains distinct.

sections.title: Some safeguards were implied, but the remedy bar was express
sections.cue: Distinguish curable silence from an unlawful limitation.
paragraphs: The backpay-only clause excluded statutory punitive damages and attorney fees and was unlawful. Foundation Health argued it applied only to contract claims because one sentence mentioned terms and covenants. The sweeping exclusion of all other remedies defeated that reading.

Discovery presented no additional incurable defect. Employees needed essential documents and witnesses, and agreeing to arbitrate FEHA implicitly promised enough discovery to vindicate it. The arbitrator could balance that need with simplicity, subject to limited review. The court did not decide whether FEHA automatically received the full statutory discovery machinery through a personal-injury provision.

The agreement similarly was read to require a written decision showing essential findings and conclusions adequate for judicial review. Reviewing a motion to compel rather than an award, the court reserved the precise review standard; it did not authorize general appellate correction of every arbitral legal error.

sections.title: The majority allocated arbitration-specific costs to the employer
paragraphs: The majority held that compulsory arbitration generally could not charge employees expenses they would not incur in court. Foundation Health had to pay forum and arbitrator costs unique to arbitration. The risk of substantial charges could deter statutory claims even if later review might undo them, so the issue belonged at the compulsion stage.

A comparative-cost mini-trial would be speculative and burdensome. Employer payment did not itself destroy neutrality; repeat-player concerns were distinct and institutional safeguards remained relevant. The statutory pro rata rule was a default displaced by the implied promise to preserve statutory rights. Thus cost silence meant employer payment and did not independently invalidate the agreement. Ordinary litigation expenses and all attorney fees were not automatically shifted.

Justice Brown, joined by Justice Chin, favored individualized apportionment. Arbitration could be cheaper overall and some employees could pay a share. Unless advance payment or a specified employee share was required, she would leave allocation to the arbitrator considering unique costs, resources, and comparative expense, with later review protecting effective vindication. She joined the judgment and most reasoning despite rejecting the bright line.

sections.title: The compulsory forum also lacked justified mutuality
sections.cue: Explain ordinary unconscionability apart from statutory rights.
paragraphs: The court required both procedural oppression or surprise and substantively harsh or one-sided terms, operating on a sliding scale. Adhesion began rather than ended the inquiry. Here an employment condition without negotiation established the procedural concern.

A stronger party could not require arbitration of the weaker party’s transaction-related claims while reserving corresponding claims for court simply for advantage. Business realities might justify asymmetry, but the employer had to establish them. This was general unconscionability, distinct from consideration: a supported promise could still be unconscionably one-sided.

For example, discharge for alleged trade-secret theft would send the employee’s termination claim to arbitration but leave the employer’s theft claim in court. Saying these supervisors rarely possessed proprietary information did not justify categorical exclusion even of rare corresponding claims. Backpay only through the award also excluded front pay available in ordinary wrongful-termination contract damages, without a comparable employer limit. Removing only the FEHA restriction would not cure that imbalance.

sections.title: Deletion could not supply the missing employer promise
sections.cue: State the severance analysis and exact judgment.
paragraphs: Civil Code section 1670.5 allowed refusal, severance, or restriction of unconscionable terms. The court favored preserving lawful purposes when collateral illegality was curable, but not arrangements permeated by an unlawful purpose. Here the combined remedy and forum defects suggested a systematic inferior forum favoring the employer. More decisively, mutuality required adding an employer duty to arbitrate, not merely deleting language; the statute did not authorize that augmentation.

The employer’s later willingness to accept mutual arbitration and full remedies was at most an unaccepted modification, not a retroactive cure. Replacing biased arbitrators rested on a separate appointment statute, and deleting post-award escape provisions involved removable terms and avoiding a reward to their drafter. The court reserved whether the damages clause alone warranted total refusal and whether its drafting had been in bad faith under then-existing law.

Mosk was joined by Chief Justice George and Justices Kennard, Baxter, and Werdegar. Brown and Chin concurred without dissenting from disposition. On August 24, 2000, the court reversed the Court of Appeal and directed it to affirm refusal to compel. It decided no discrimination claim, awarded no damages, and required no arbitration under a judicially rewritten contract.
